title: Bomb Lab & GDB
example:
Opening your bomb
Reading assembly
Breakpoints and memory inspection
notes: Use iLab for the live demonstration. Demonstrate debugging technique using the separate example.c exercise before inspecting a bomb.

title: The Bomb Lab
lead:
A binary bomb is an executable with phases that check your input.

A correct line defuses a phase. An incorrect line reaches the explosion path.

Your job is to infer the checks from the machine code.
example:
Read the phase
Identify the required input format
Follow the conditions
Explain a candidate input
Test with breakpoints
caption: Check Canvas for the deadline, scoring, and submission instructions. Explosions may be recorded.
notes: Source: CS:APP Bomb Lab instructor README supplied by the TA, overview and solving sections. The supplied document describes multiple deployment modes, so do not announce a particular penalty or grading mechanism without the current student handout.

title: Everyone has a unique bomb
lead:
Your bomb has its own constants and phase variants.

The recitation demo may have different strings, numbers, and addresses.

Use your own disassembly to justify each input.
example:
Same tools
Different executable
Different checks

A value from the demo may fail
in your bomb.
notes: Source: supplied CS:APP instructor README, randomized phase variants and parameterized constants. The TA explicitly states that every student will receive a unique bomb. Do not display the private phase-change notes or a staff solution.

title: The student folder
lead:
bomb is the executable you investigate.

bomb.c shows the main program and how it reads input. It may omit the phase implementations.

README and ID identify your assigned bomb.
example:
Typical student files

bomb
bomb.c
README
ID

ls
less bomb.c
caption: Your downloaded folder may differ. Keep the supplied executable intact.
notes: Source: supplied CS:APP instructor README, student archive contents. The TA screenshot shows a staff build folder with additional files. Those extra source and solution artifacts are not part of the student workflow and are deliberately excluded. In less, use q to return to the shell.

title: Opening the bomb on iLab
lead:
Download instructions for your assigned bomb will be on the course markup.

Follow those instructions on iLab, then extract the archive and open your bomb in GDB.

Replace N with your bomb number. Use the actual archive and folder names.
example:
# On iLab, after downloading
tar xvf bombN.tar
cd bombN
ls
cat README
gdb ./bomb
caption: The shell runs tar and gdb. The (gdb) prompt accepts debugger commands.
notes: The TA states that download instructions will appear on the course markup; use those instructions rather than assuming a local download and scp workflow. Do not invent a wget URL. tar xvf handles a .tar archive; use the course's exact filename and archive format. These are example names. Source for the student tar archive: supplied instructor README.

title: C code and assembly
lead:
For C source you own, gcc -S produces an assembly file.

-g adds debugger information. -O0 keeps optimization off for this exercise.

The bomb already contains machine code. Inspect that executable directly.
example:
# With the supplied example.c
gcc -O0 -S example.c -o example.s
less example.s

# A separate executable for GDB
gcc -g -O0 example.c -o example
gdb ./example
caption: Compiling bomb.c alone may fail because the phase code is missing.
notes: Download example.c from the presentation toolbar and put it in an iLab practice directory. It defines transform(x) = 3*x + 2, called with 4. In GDB, break transform, run, print x, disassemble transform, and stepi. Its main returns success when the computed result is 14. Sources: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html and https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Debugging-Options.html .

title: Assembly from the executable
lead:
objdump displays machine instructions without running the bomb.

In GDB, disassemble displays one function.

Use AT&T syntax consistently with the earlier recitations.
example:
# Shell
objdump -d bomb > bomb-disassembly.txt
less bomb-disassembly.txt

# Inside GDB
set disassembly-flavor att
info functions phase_
disassemble phase_1
caption: Function names depend on your executable. Use the symbols it actually provides.
notes: Sources: https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/binutils/objdump.html and https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Machine-Code.html . The > operator writes objdump output to a text file. less supports /phase_1 to search and q to quit. GDB function names require available symbols. Compiler-generated .s text and disassembly can differ in formatting and addresses.

title: The first GDB session
lead:
Set breakpoints before running. Stop at the phase entry and inspect its instructions.

A breakpoint on explode_bomb gives an extra stopping point if execution reaches it.

At that breakpoint, inspect and stop the run.
example:
(gdb) break phase_1
(gdb) break explode_bomb
(gdb) info breakpoints
(gdb) run

# At the phase breakpoint
(gdb) disassemble phase_1
(gdb) x/i $pc
caption: A breakpoint pauses execution. Continuing from explode_bomb can execute the failure routine.
notes: Use the actual symbol names in the assigned executable. A phase-entry breakpoint may occur after read_line has already requested input. Distinguish input typed to the running bomb from commands typed at (gdb). A breakpoint at explode_bomb is a backup, not a promise that all versions avoid reporting a failure. Do not step through or continue the explosion routine. Use kill to stop the inferior, then inspect and restart. Source: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Set-Breaks.html .

title: Managing breakpoints
lead:
Break at a function or at a specific instruction address.

GDB assigns a number to each breakpoint. Use that number to disable or delete it.

Choose addresses from your current disassembly.
example:
break phase_2
break *ADDRESS
info breakpoints

disable 2
enable 2
delete 2

help break
caption: Replace ADDRESS with a real address. Breakpoint numbers may differ in your session.
notes: Source: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Set-Breaks.html . Show one address breakpoint live using an address copied from the student's running process. Absolute addresses may change across runs under address randomization. Prefer function breakpoints when possible. explain that b, info b, and d are common abbreviations but use full commands when teaching.

title: Stepping through instructions
lead:
si executes one machine instruction and enters calls. ni executes one instruction and steps over calls.

Stepping over a call still runs the function.

Source commands step and next operate on source lines when debug information exists.
example:
si         # stepi
ni         # nexti
x/i $pc    # current instruction

continue   # run until next stop
run        # restart from the beginning
kill       # stop the running program
quit       # leave GDB
caption: Inspect the destination of a call before using ni or continue.
notes: Source: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Continuing-and-Stepping.html . A breakpoint or signal can interrupt stepping. finish runs until the current function returns and can also execute a failure path, so it is not a safe substitute for understanding the function. Ctrl+C pauses a running program. kill terminates the inferior while keeping GDB open. run may ask whether to restart if a program is already active.

title: Registers and memory in GDB
lead:
print shows a value. x examines memory at an address.

Choose the display format to match the data: strings, integers, or pointers.

In GDB, register names begin with $. In AT&T assembly, they begin with %.
example:
info registers rax rdi rsi rsp
p/x $rax       # register in hex
p/d $rax       # register in decimal
x/s $rdi       # string at address
x/4dw $rsp     # four 4-byte integers
x/2gx $rsp     # two 8-byte values
x/5i $pc       # five instructions
caption: Use x/s only when the register holds a readable string address.
notes: Sources: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Memory.html and https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Registers.html . x/4dw: 4 units, decimal format, word units of 4 bytes. x/2gx: 2 units, 8-byte giant words, hexadecimal format. p/d displays the register as a signed integer according to its type. For parsed 32-bit results, p/d $eax can be more appropriate. On System V AMD64, integer and pointer arguments commonly begin in rdi and rsi, and integer return values use rax/eax. Only interpret arguments at the appropriate call boundary.

title: An address or its contents
lead:
A register can hold a number or an address. mov copies the operand you specify.

A parenthesized source operand in mov loads the contents at that address.

lea computes an address without reading its contents.
example:
# Suppose rbx = 0x2000
# memory[0x2000] contains 37

movq %rbx, %rax     # rax = 0x2000
movq (%rbx), %rax   # rax = 37
leaq 8(%rbx), %rax  # rax = 0x2008

# GDB checks
p/x $rbx
x/gd $rbx
caption: Toy values for this example. Addresses and contents in your bomb will differ.
notes: Connect to the earlier house-address discussion: copying the address versus fetching the contents. lea is often used to form pointers to strings or stack slots before a helper call. x/gd reads an 8-byte value and formats it as signed decimal. Memory command reference: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Memory.html .

title: Input formats and comparisons
lead:
Identify what the program parses before solving the checks.

A parsing helper may check how many fields it read. A later comparison checks their values.

Read the comparison and the branch together.
example:
# Toy input format
"%d %c"     # integer, then character

# Toy value check
cmp $9, %eax
jne failure

To avoid this branch, eax must be 9.
caption: A parsed-field count and a parsed value answer different questions.
notes: Use this as a method hint without associating any helper or input format with a specific phase. Inspect a format-string pointer at the relevant parsing call and inspect the return count afterward. cmp source,destination sets flags as if computing destination - source. jne follows unequal values. The spaces in a scanf-family format matter because %c alone does not skip whitespace. The format and constant here are invented for teaching and are not phase answers.

title: Loops and lookup tables
lead:
For a loop, track the index and which earlier elements the code reads.

For a table, find the base address, entry size, and index bounds.

A mask can reduce an input before the program uses it as an index.
example:
Loop notes
index    values read    value written

Address calculation
base + index * element_size

After a mask
track the masked index
caption: Derive the relationship from the instructions. Familiar-looking sequences can use different rules.
notes: Board activity: make a blank trace table and fill one iteration with the room. Look at the displacement and index expressions to distinguish dependencies on different earlier entries. Tables can contain values or code addresses, so inspect the instructions that consume each entry. General method hints only. Do not show private phase variants, constants, or recurrence sequences from the staff notes.

title: Calls and pointer structures
lead:
For recursive code, identify the stopping condition and how each call changes its arguments.

For pointer structures, distinguish a node's value from its next pointer.

Write down each address you visit before following the next link.
example:
Recursive trace
arguments    base case    return value

Pointer trace
node address    data    next address

Array index and node value
may represent different things.
caption: Assembly offsets reveal which field the program reads and how it uses that field.
notes: Offer this as a broad strategy for later phases. Do not identify any private algorithm, ordering direction, tree values, or hidden-phase trigger. Inspect comparisons to infer what a value means instead of assuming an index equals the stored data. bt can show the call chain when paused in recursion.

title: Saving confirmed inputs
lead:
Keep a separate text file with one confirmed phase input per line, in order.

Read bomb.c to check whether your version accepts that file as a command-line argument.

Keep your own notes on why each line passes.
example:
# If bomb.c supports a filename
(gdb) run answers.txt

# Otherwise, stdin redirection
(gdb) run < answers.txt

# Breakpoints remain in this session
(gdb) info breakpoints
caption: An argument file and stdin redirection handle end-of-file differently. Check your version before relying on either.
notes: The standard CS:APP driver often accepts a filename and switches to interactive input when that file ends, while stdin redirection may terminate at EOF. Verify the supplied bomb.c instead of promising that behavior for every version. Do not include placeholders or guessed lines in a replay file. Source for input redirection and distinct deployment modes: supplied instructor README. GDB run syntax: https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Arguments.html and https://sourceware.org/gdb/current/onlinedocs/gdb.html/Input_002fOutput.html .

title: A phase investigation
lead:
Pause at the phase entry.

Identify the input format and failure branches.

Track the registers or memory that each check uses.

Test a candidate only after you can explain it.
example:
Useful notes to keep

Function and instruction address
Input fields
Condition required to pass
Observed register or memory values
Reason for the candidate input
caption: When asking for help, bring the exact instruction and your current interpretation.
notes: Close with a short live demonstration on the student's own assigned executable. If execution reaches the failure routine breakpoint, inspect the caller with bt and disassemble, then kill and restart after correcting the reasoning. The goal is understanding each check rather than changing registers or patching the executable to skip it.
